snippet.title: No Income Tax? How the U.S. Paid Its Bills Before 1913
snippet.description:
Before 1913, the United States didn’t rely on income tax to fund the government. So how did it pay its bills? This video explores the pre-income tax era, when federal revenue came mainly from tariffs, excise taxes, and land sales.

Tariffs on imported goods were the largest source of income, making trade policy a central part of government finance. Excise taxes on products like alcohol and tobacco also contributed significantly. While this system worked in a smaller economy, it had limitations as the country expanded and government spending increased.

This video breaks down how early U.S. finances operated, why the income tax was eventually introduced, and what changed after 1913 that reshaped the modern economic system.

snippet.title: The $83 Trap: Why Silver Collapsed to $75
snippet.description:
Silver’s move from $83 down to $75 caught many traders off guard, but sharp reversals often reveal more about positioning than price alone. What looked like a breakout above $83 quickly turned into a failed extension—triggering liquidation and momentum-driven selling.

When markets push above resistance without sustained volume or follow-through buying, liquidity gaps can form, leaving late entrants vulnerable. As upside momentum stalled, stop-loss clusters and leveraged positions accelerated the drop toward $75.

In this video, we break down why the $83 level became a trap zone, how failed breakouts typically unwind, and what structural signals emerged during the decline. Understanding exhaustion moves and order-flow imbalance helps separate technical resets from deeper trend shifts.

The broader takeaway centers on volatility cycles. After rapid declines, markets often enter rebalancing phases where liquidity rebuilds and positioning resets. Whether $75 becomes stabilization or continuation depends on participation and demand absorption.

Watch till the end to understand how the $83 rejection led to a swift move lower, what professionals monitor after failed breakouts, and how to approach silver during high-volatility transitions.

snippet.title: Crash Course Geology Preview
snippet.description:
Welcome to Crash Course Geology! Over the course of 25 episodes, Sage will introduce you to the incredible geological forces, cycles, and processes that shape our world. This series will explore how geology touches all of our lives — and connects us to a much bigger story.

Course Description
In 25 episodes, we’re going to learn about geology—the study of Earth’s physical structure and processes. Our host, Sage, will teach you about the geological forces and cycles that shape our planet’s past, present, and future. 

This content is based on an introductory university-level curriculum. By the end of this course, you should be able to: 

Trace Earth’s development from its earliest periods to its current structure
Understand the forces of plate tectonics and how they shape Earth’s landscape
Describe the formation of geologic elements like minerals, rocks, and gems 
Identify geologic forces and cycles that impact the earth, while dispelling myths about extreme geological hazards
Learn what geology reveals about Earth’s distant past and what it can teach us about our current changing climate
Explore the geology of other planets within the context of Earth’s unique and common qualities and phenomena
Become familiar with different specialities within geology and what different types of geologists do

Key texts cited include:
Marshak, Stephen. 2021. Earth: Portrait of a Planet, Seventh Edition.
Babcock, Loren E. 2009. Gemstones and Precious Metals.

snippet.title: The $38 Trillion Debt Trick Explained
snippet.description:
The U.S. doesn’t “pay off” $38 trillion in debt — it manages it through structure. This video explains how rollover cycles, maturity extension, inflation dilution, and steady Treasury issuance keep the system functioning without sudden collapse. Sovereign debt operates differently than household debt: it’s refinanced, not retired.

The real mechanism isn’t cancellation — it’s time and liquidity. As older debt matures, it’s replaced with new issuance. Inflation reduces the real burden over time, while reserve demand and deep capital markets absorb supply. The constraint isn’t the headline number — it’s interest expense, confidence, and liquidity conditions.

This video breaks down how large sovereign debts are sustained, why refinancing matters more than repayment, and what would signal when debt management shifts into debt stress.

• The powerful banks that helped finance Nazi Germany
• The secret financial networks that survived World War II
• What happened to Nazi industrial money after 1945
• The controversial role of European banks during the war
• How wartime financial systems influenced modern Europe

This video explores historical records, economic history, and investigative research to uncover one of the most controversial financial legacies of the 20th century.

History often focuses on battles and political leaders—but behind every war lies a powerful financial system.

And sometimes… that system never truly disappears.

snippet.description:
John D. Rockefeller was once the richest man in modern history. At his peak, his fortune controlled nearly 90% of the American oil industry through his company Standard Oil.

But the real story is not just about oil.

The true secret behind Rockefeller’s wealth was the system he created — a powerful combination of monopolies, strategic investments, trusts, and global influence. Even after Standard Oil was broken up in 1911, the Rockefeller financial network continued to grow.

Many of today’s biggest corporations — including major energy companies and financial institutions — trace their roots back to the Rockefeller empire.

In this documentary, we explore:

• How John D. Rockefeller built Standard Oil
• The monopoly strategy that changed capitalism forever
